chunks: Buck power bridge type and why. The question: What type of power bridge is often implemented? Why?
The usual bridge in a buck is a half bridge of two N-channel MOSFETs. The top one connects the switch node to the input, and the bottom one connects it to ground.
They turn on in turn, never together. The bottom one replaces the diode, and both are N-type because that type is the better transistor.
Picture a toggle switch that connects one wire either to the high supply or to ground, always one or the other. That wire is the switch node.
The controller flips the toggle many times a second. Between flips there is a very short pause, so the two connections never touch.
Two NFETs stacked between V in and ground. The midpoint is SW. Q 1 's source is the switch node, so its gate must be driven relative to SW, not relative to ground.
Q 2 's source is ground, so it is easy to drive.
Half bridge: two transistors in a stack, with the switch node between them. NFET / MOSFET: a transistor switched by its gate voltage; N-type has lower resistance for its size.
Synchronous rectification: using a transistor in place of the diode ("Synchronous rectification pros and cons").
Dead time: the short pause when both transistors are off ("Shoot-through and dead time"). R DS(on) : a transistor's resistance when fully on.
A 2 amps inductor current flows through the bottom device while the top is off. A Schottky diode with a 0. 5 volts drop wastes 0. 5 times 2 equals 1 watts while it conducts.
A transistor with 10 milliohms wastes only 2 squared times 0. 01 equals 0. 04 watts. That is why the bottom device is a transistor. That is the whole idea.
"Most buck converters use a half bridge of two NFETs with synchronous rectification: a high-side NFET to V in and a low-side NFET to ground, driven complementary with dead time.
The low-side FET replaces the diode because I times R DS(on) is far below a diode's fixed 0. 3 to 0. 7 volts drop, which matters most at low output voltage and high current.
NFETs on both sides because electrons are more mobile than holes, so an NFET has about two to three times lower on-resistance per area.
The cost is a bootstrap driver and dead-time control."
